title: Permanent dentition
description: Diseases and complications of the adult dentition that a GDP diagnoses and treats.

problems.description: Sharp pain on cold or sweet that stops the moment the stimulus is gone. Usually one tooth, though the patient often can't say which one.
problems.etiology:
The pulp gets irritated by three things: caries, trauma, and damage from a previous filling or procedure [1].

None need to be dramatic on their own. The effects are cumulative — small insults (bacterial, thermal, chemical, traumatic) add up, and once they cross a threshold the pulp inflames and starts to hurt [2].

The interesting bit: what decides whether the pulp recovers is its **blood supply**, not its nerve supply [3]. The diagnostic consequence:

- Vitality tests are actually sensibility tests — they check the nerve, not the pulp itself.
- No clinical test gives you a 100% accurate read of pulp status.
- The only method that does is histological section, which isn't an option in a living tooth [3].
problems.presentation:
What you'll typically hear:

- Quick, sharp jab of pain on cold, hot, or sweet.
- Gone within seconds of the stimulus being removed [4].
- Patient often can't pin down exactly which tooth — the pulp has no proprioceptive nerves [5].
- Pain won't cross the midline. If the patient is jumping between left and right, the cause is something else [5].
- No pain on biting. No tenderness over the gum above the tooth [6].
problems.results:
- **Cold test**: exaggerated response — a noticeably louder reaction than the neighbouring teeth [7].
- **Inspect**: usually a fresh carious cavity or a leaking restoration [7].
- **Percussion**: not tender. TTP would push you toward apical involvement, so its absence keeps you on a pulpitis diagnosis [7].
- **Radiograph**: apical tissues look normal. Lamina dura intact, no widening of the PDL space [8].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The single most useful question to ask yourself: **does the pain stop the moment the stimulus is gone?**

- Yes → reversible.
- No (lingers, spontaneous, or radiates) → irreversible [9].

Other tells:

- Short, repeated attacks of pain (rather than continuous severe pain) point to reversible. Pulp is probably still saveable if you treat the cause now [6].
- Poor localisation is normal for pulpal pain. On its own it tells you nothing about reversibility — don't be thrown by it [5].
problems.treatment:
The principle is straightforward: **find the cause and take it away.**

- Caries → remove it and restore.
- Leaking filling → redo it.
- Can't do a definitive restoration in one visit? Place a sedative dressing like ZOE to settle things and buy time [10].

If the cavity is deep but the pulp isn't actually exposed (dentine still over the pulp), do an **indirect pulp cap**. The sequence:

- Rubber dam on.
- Selective caries removal at the floor and axial wall. Leave a thin layer of stained but firm dentine over the pulp rather than risk an exposure chasing the last of the caries.
- Disinfect the deep cavity with sodium hypochlorite 0.5–5% on a cotton pellet (excess wrung out) for 30 seconds to a minute.
- Dry it.
- Cover the deepest part with a calcium silicate cement. Calcium hydroxide sealed under GIC or RMGIC works if no CSC is available.
- Place the definitive restoration over the top and keep the tooth under review [11].
problems.prognosis:
- Catch it early, treat the cause → the pulp settles [6].
- Leave it → the lesion enlarges over months, the pulpitis turns irreversible, and by the time the patient comes back the pulp may already be necrotic. The only option left is RCT on a dead pulp [12].

**Rule of thumb** when you can't quite decide: treat as reversible. RCT can always be started later if symptoms tell you you've been too conservative — just warn the patient upfront [13].

citations.quote: The pulp is under threat from three main sources: carious attack, trauma and iatrogenic damage (Bjørndal et al 2019).
citations.source: BES Guidelines 2022 — Vital Pulp Therapy, p.43

citations.quote: The pulp may be subject to a wide variety of insults (e.g. bacterial, thermal, chemical, traumatic), the effects of which are cumulative and can ultimately lead to inflammation in the pulp (pulpitis) and pain.
The ability of the pulp to recover from injury depends upon its blood supply, not the nerve supply, which must be borne in mind when vitality (sensibility) testing is carried out
Fleeting sensitivity/pain to hot, cold, or sweet with immediate onset. Pain is usually sharp and may be difficult to locate. Quickly subsides after removal of the stimulus.

The dental pulp does not contain any proprioceptive nerve endings, therefore a characteristic of pulpal pain is that the patient is unable to localize the affected tooth but the pain does not cross the midline.

The classic history of acute pulpitis and repeated attacks of pain – as opposed to continuous severe pain – probably indicates that the pulp can be preserved if the caries is treated. The fact that there is no pain on biting and no tenderness over the roots also suggests a reversible pulpitis and helps exclude periapical periodontitis.
Exaggerated response to pulp testing. Carious cavity/leaking restoration. Tooth not tender to percussion.
Short, sharp sensitivity to cold • Localised to the affected tooth • Questionable restoration, coronal fracture • Normal appearance of apical tissues
citations.source: BES Guidelines 2022 — Examination and Diagnosis, Table 1.1

citations.quote: Reversible pulpitis: Pain or discomfort initiated by a stimulus such as cold or sweet which resolves shortly after the stimulus is removed. Irreversible pulpitis: More intense pain that can be spontaneous or radiating which is longer lasting and lingers after removal of stimulus.
citations.source: BES Guidelines 2022 — Vital Pulp Therapy, p.43

citations.quote: Remove any caries present and restore or place a sedative dressing (e.g. ZOE) or permanent restoration with suitable pulp protection.

The cavity should be disinfected using cotton pellets soaked (removing gross excess) ideally with sodium hypochlorite (0.5-5%) for 30 seconds to one minute. Having dried this, the deepest part of the cavity closest to the pulp should ideally be covered with a CSC but calcium hydroxide is suitable if an appropriate CSC is not available. If calcium hydroxide is used it should be sealed with glass ionomer cement (GIC) or a resin glass ionomer cement (RMGIC).
citations.source: BES Guidelines 2022 — Vital Pulp Therapy, p.45 (indirect pulp capping)

citations.quote: When the pain started 8 months ago, the carious lesion would have been smaller and the pulpitis reversible. If it had been treated preventively and operatively at that stage by the oral healthcare team, it is high likely that any endodontic treatment would now be required for a necrotic pulp.
If in doubt, treat as for reversible pulpitis. Can always institute RCT later; however, be sure to warn the patient of a possible further need for Rx.
